title: Leaders Who Own All of the Key Decisions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article critiques leaders and leadership teams who insist on retaining veto power over nearly every decision, even ones nominally delegated to others. It describes the corrosive effects: disengaged, apathetic team members, junior leaders who never build real credibility, and a culture where colleagues learn to 'shop' unpopular decisions back up the chain in hopes of a reversal. In contrast, the piece describes leaders who clearly define which decisions they own, delegate the rest genuinely, and decline to intervene unless something is going seriously wrong, thereby building the credibility and growth of the leaders beneath them.
points: Leaders who retain veto power over delegated decisions create disengaged, apathetic teams.
One organization's leadership team was nicknamed 'the deciders,' a label meant as criticism, not praise.
Team members learn to 'shop' unpopular decisions back to a leader known to reverse them.
The best leaders clearly define which decisions they own and genuinely hand off the rest.
Refusing to interfere in delegated decisions builds the credibility and growth of junior leaders.
quotes: Some leaders can’t give up control or don’t feel comfortable unless they own all the important decisions for the team or organization.
In one well-known organization where the management team controls nearly every call, the senior team is known as “the deciders” by their colleagues throughout the enterprise.
The more team members succeed in their efforts to sway decisions they don’t like, the longer the line of people outside the leader’s door.
Instead, they clearly lay out what decisions they own and they push down decisions that are better made by others.
Leaders who refrain from influencing decisions they don’t own soon see the line of team members who need to speak with them disappear.
As they share the responsibilities of leadership with other leaders, they empower them to learn and grow as leaders.
